messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: vector/matrix ctors for var
parts:
It's a bit different for vars. With these three functions:

|
double fun1(const Matrix<var,Dynamic,1>& x) {
Matrix<var,Dynamic,1> y(x);
return y(2).val();
}
double fun2(const Matrix<var,Dynamic,1>& x) {
Matrix<var,Dynamic,1> y(x.size());
std::memcpy(&y(0),&x(0),x.size() * sizeof(double));
return y(2).val();
}
double fun3(const Matrix<var,Dynamic,1>& x) {
std::vector<var> y(&x(0),&x(0) + x.size());
return y[2].val();
}
|

the proportion of time taken is:

fun1: 46%
fun2: 30%
fun3: 24%

Oddly, memcpy is only taking about 20% of the time
spent in fun2. So I can't figure out why fun3 isn't
a whole lot faster.

This is all using clang++ -O3, by the way, with the
Stan libs also compiled with the same flags.

And you can see it's using the sse42 move
functionality.

I'm having a bit of trouble understanding the profiler output.
I'm only guessing at fun3 time because it doesn't show up at
all --- it's just that fun1 + fun2 take 76% of the time.
The other time seems to be missing. I'm attaching a screen
shot to show what I mean.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vector/matrix ctors for var
parts:
OK, I think I sorted out what's going on with
these by selecting the "invert call tree" checkbox
under "Call Tree" on the left and then sorting
by Self time. It's still confusing that it lists
some of the time under main() and some under each
of the functions.

So I just went and instrumented the code to make sure
I was interpreting the profile correctly. I get:

fun1: 27s Eigen vector copy ctor
fun2: 17s Eigen vector size ctor + memcpy
fun3: 13s std::vector iterator ctor

for the following:

> double fun1(const Matrix<var,Dynamic,1>& x) {
> Matrix<var,Dynamic,1> y(x);
> return y(2).val();
> }
> double fun2(const Matrix<var,Dynamic,1>& x) {
> Matrix<var,Dynamic,1> y(x.size());
> std::memcpy(&y(0),&x(0),x.size() * sizeof(double));
> return y(2).val();
> }
> double fun3(const Matrix<var,Dynamic,1>& x) {
> std::vector<var> y(&x(0),&x(0) + x.size());
> return y[2].val();
> }
> |

I also checked and the size ctor in fun2() only allocates
the memory, it doesn't actually fill in values. So we
don't get extraneous values on the autodiff stack using var.

So if copy ctors for Eigen vectors are taking up too much time,
I'd just rewrite them as in fun2. It's still not as fast
as std::vector, but there's no Eigen Matrix ctor that takes in
either the memory for the vector elements or an iterator.

- Bob

Your version #3 is not correct, you have to use y.insert(y.begin(),

that in some cases clang is able to optimize away memcpy when the copy
is actually not necessary. This is the case in the attached file.

gael

On Thu, May 30, 2013 at 4:58 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> We refactored our application to use Eigen column vectors
> instead of std::vector and observed a fairly significant
> slowdown. Profiling pointed to the copy constructor for
> Eigen vectors, so I'm wondering if there's something we're
> missing. Here's what I tried.
>
> To copy a column vector
>
> Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> x;
>
> there's the obvious copy constructor:
>
> 1. Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> y(x);
>
> or the direct sizing + memcpy approach:
>
> 2. Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> y(x.size());
> std::memcpy(&y(0),&x(0),x.size() * sizeof(double));
>
> By comparison, we can use an iterator based on the
> memory used for x's values to construct a standard
> vector:
>
> 3. std::vector<double> y(&x(0),&x(0) + x.size());
>
> I timed each version by repeatedly calling it, and found
> the times varied pretty widely:
>
> 1. 26s
> 2. 17s
> 3. 14s
>
> For Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> on the other hand, the
> copy constructor and the memcpy versions took about the same
> time.
>
> Is there a faster way to copy vectors? I'm guessing we'll have
> the same issue if I were to pass in references, resize them and
> then assign (like copy ctor) or memcpy.
>
> This was using clang++ -O3 on a Macbook Pro with i7 CPU and clang
> version:
>
> Apple clang version 4.1 (tags/Apple/clang-421.11.66) (based on LLVM
> 3.1svn)
> Target: x86_64-apple-darwin12.3.0
>
> - Bob
>
>

ctor.cpp

#include <Eigen/Dense>
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
#include <bench/BenchTimer.h>

using namespace Eigen;

EIGEN_DONT_INLINE
double* cp1(const VectorXd& A, int i = 0)
{
VectorXd B(A);
return &B(i);
}

EIGEN_DONT_INLINE
double* cp2(const VectorXd& A, int i = 0)
{
VectorXd B(A.size());
std::memcpy(B.data(), A.data(), A.size()*sizeof(double));
return &B(i);
}

EIGEN_DONT_INLINE
double* cp3(const VectorXd& A, int i = 0)
{
std::vector<double> B;
B.insert(B.begin(), A.data(), A.data()+A.size());
return &B[i];
}

int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
using namespace std;

BenchTimer t1,t2,t3;
int tries = 10;
int rep = 1000;
int n = 100000;
VectorXd A(n);
A.setRandom();
BENCH(t1,tries,rep,cp1(A));
BENCH(t2,tries,rep,cp2(A));
BENCH(t3,tries,rep,cp3(A));
cout << t1.best() << " ; " << t2.best() << " ; " << t3.best() << endl;
}

There have been some changes in the autodiff code for multivariate model that may have made chain() a little slower, but it should balance out with reduced computation elsewhere.  Plus, most of the BUGS models don't use the multivariate distributions, so it shouldn't have such a consistent across the board hit.

I would benchmark grad_log_prob() for a single model to see if it's there.

And yeah, between calls to check_range, check_not_nan, etc, there is a big speedup to be had if we can ever reduce the need for repeatedly checking variables like this.

Cheers,
Marcus

}

EIGEN_DONT_INLINE
double* cp2(const VectorXd& A, int i = 0)
{
  VectorXd B(A.size());

On 5/31/13 4:15 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> You need to store rho and the state (at the very least momentum) at the boundary of each subtree -- maybe that scales as log(n)? I'm pretty sure the code is as tight as it can be without appealing to pools or the like.

Imisread n as the number of leapfrog steps,
not the depth.

Let's switch to the NUTS arXiv paper notation, where
j is tree depth and 2^j the number of leaf nodes (leapfrog
steps are in one-one correspondence with leaf nodes).

Section 3.1.2 of the paper provides a O(j) memory algorithm. It's a pretty
simple induction that assumes you only store the sample that
would be produced (if any) from each subtree and its (position,momentum)
at the endpoints. Because NUTS only checks that the ends of
each subtree don't make a U-turn, once you've completed a subtree
and chosen a sample from it, you never need to look inside it again.

Of course, it's still O(2^j) time because we do have to do each
leapfrog step.

If you're using O(j^2) for some reason, that could account
for the increased number of objects you're finding in the profiles.

I'm looking at it NUTS now. I'm still trying to figure out
if we can get away from static casting ps points.

To see that memory is O(j) for a depth j tree, just use
a simple induction.

Base step: You can build a depth 0 tree (single node) in
constant time --- there's nothing to build.

Inductive step: Suppose you can build a depth n tree in
memory size O(n). To build a depth (n + 1) tree, you need to
first build a depth n tree for the first half, which will
take O(n) memory. Then you trim it down to its edges, so you're
now using a constant amount of memory and have maxed out at O(n).
Now build the depth n tree making up the second half of the
depth (n + 1) tree. That will take O(n) memory. Adding the
constant memory required to be stored for the first half, we
get O(n + 1) total.

- Bob

On 6/1/13 2:36 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

>
> Keep an eye on the fast_constructor branch, I've been cleaning up base_nuts.hpp here, too.
That's what I'm looking at.

> I think the right approach to avoiding static casts is to introduce copy constructors
> and operator= for the base class and then just call them explicitly when manipulating a derived class.

Why not just hold references to the base class. Then
all the virtual functions do what you want them to do rather
than being sliced as the static cast does. And it gets away
from all the ugly pointers in the code, too. For example, consider

ps_point* z = 0;
Eigen::VectorXd* rho = 0;

if (this->_rand_uniform() > 0.5)
{
z = &z_plus;
rho = &rho_plus;
util.sign = 1;
}
else
{
z = &z_minus;
rho = &rho_minus;
util.sign = -1;
}

this->_z.copy_base(*z);

int n_valid_subtree = build_tree(_depth, *rho, 0, z_propose, util);

*z = static_cast<ps_point>(this->_z);


You don't need the init to 0 here, as they'll get set whichever
way you go through the branch.

The above could be recoded as follows using references (and less
vertical space) as:

ps_point& z = &z_plus;
Eigen::VectorXd& rho = &rho_plus
if (this->_rand_uniform() > 0.5) {
util.sign = 1;
} else {
z = &z_minus;
rho = &rho_minus;
util.sign = -1;
}
this->_z = z;
int n_valid_subtree = build_tree(_depth, rho, 0, z_propose, util);
z = &(this->z_);

And there's still something fishy about having to use "this->" that
I don't understand.

If util.sign is used to multiply doubles, it should probably be
a double to avoid having to do the promotion on the fly.

- Bob
